text: Two studies implicate mammalian RAD52 in break-induced replication (BIR) repair of collapsed DNA replication forks. A targeted siRNA screen for genes inhibiting G1-to-S progression under oncogenic cyclin E overexpression identified RAD52—dispensable for normal mouse development—as a top hit. In cells with oncogene- or chemical-induced fork collapse, Rad52 localized to DNA replication stress (DRS) foci; siRNA depletion or CRISPR/Cas9 knockout compromised fork restart and caused DNA damage. In cancer-prone heterozygous APC mutant mice, homozygous Rad52 deletion suppressed tumor growth and prolonged lifespan. Separately, mitotic DNA synthesis (MiDAS) at human telomeres, which resemble common fragile sites (CFSs), is widespread across cell lines regardless of telomerase- or ALT-based maintenance, requires RAD52, and—unlike CFS-associated MiDAS—does not require the MUS81-EME1 endonuclease. RAD52-dependent BIR thus helps cancer cells tolerate replication stress at collapsed forks and telomeres.
